3 US Presidential Election Polling via Frequentist Methods

We will soon turn our attention back to our second motivational example, that of US Presidential election polling, but first we must do some revision and define our notation.

3.1 Random Variables, Expectation & Variance: Revision and Notation

3.1.1 Discrete Random Variables

  • •

    A discrete random variable X is a variable which can take a finite (or countable) set of different numerical values x1,x2,⋯∈𝒳, according to the different possible outcomes of an experiment or random phenomenon.

  • •

    We denote the probability mass function (p.m.f), also called the probability function (p.f.) (see for example DeGroot & Schervish), as

    f⁢(x)=P⁢(X=x),for all⁢x∈𝒳. (7)
  • •

    Note that sometimes the probability mass function is denoted p⁢(x), but it will be convenient for us to use f⁢(x) to be more in alignment with the continuous case.

Example: Discrete Random Variables

Possible values, x 0 1 2 3 4 5
Probabilities, P⁢(X=x) 0.33 0.41 0.20 0.05 0.01 0.00

Since the possible values for X are exhaustive and mutually exclusive, the probability that X takes one of the values within a specific set can be calculated using the addition law for disjoint events. For example:

P⁢(X∈{1,3})=P⁢(X=1⁢or⁢X=3)=P⁢(X=1)+P⁢(X=3)=0.41+ 0.05=0.46
  • •

    Often, a discrete random variable has a distribution that depends on an external parameter.

Definition: The Poisson Distribution

The Poisson distribution depends on the parameter λ. We write X∼P⁢o⁢(λ) and denote its p.m.f. as

f⁢(x|λ)=P⁢(X=x)={e−λ⁢λxx!for⁢x=0,1,2,…0otherwise. (8)
  • •

    Note the new notation when specifying a specific probability distribution above: f⁢(x|λ), to be read as “f of x given λ”. This is needed because in order for us to calculate the probability mass function for the Poisson distribution we need to be told (i.e. given) the value of λ. If λ was uncertain, which it will be later in the course, then this would affect our p.m.f of X, hence we cannot just use the notation f⁢(x) here.

  • •

    This will also allow us to use Bayes theorem with these objects too!

3.1.2 Expectation and Variance of Discrete Random Variables

  • •

    The expected value (or expectation) of a discrete random variable X is defined as

    E⁢[X]=∑x∈𝒳x⁢P⁢(X=x)=∑x∈𝒳x⁢f⁢(x), (9)

    that is, we take the weighted average of X, where the weights are the corresponding probabilities.

  • •

    The expected value of any function h⁢(X) of X is defined to be

    E⁢[h⁢(X)]=∑x∈𝒳h⁢(x)⁢P⁢(X=x)=∑x∈𝒳h⁢(x)⁢f⁢(x), (10)

    i.e. a weighted average of the function. For example, the expected value of X2 is

    E⁢[X2]=∑x∈𝒳x2⁢f⁢(x). (11)
  • •

    The variance of a random variable is defined to be

    Var⁢[X] = E⁢[(X−E⁢[X])2] (12)
    = E⁢[X2]−(E⁢[X])2. (13)

    Observe that the variance measures the theoretical average of the distance of the values of the random variable X from its central value as measured by the expected value. In this way, the variance measures the spread of values of a random variable.

  • •

    The standard deviation of a random variable is just the square root of the variance:

    SD⁢[X]=Var⁢[X]. (14)

Example: Discrete Random Variables

We can calculate the expectation and variance for random variable X with probability mass function as given by the table in the previous section as follows:

E⁢[X] = ∑x∈𝒳x⁢P⁢(X=x)
= 0×0.33+1×0.41+2×0.20+3×0.05+4×0.01=1
E⁢[X2] = 02×0.33+12×0.41+22×0.20+32×0.05+42×0.01=1.82
Var⁢[X] = E⁢[X2]−(E⁢[X])2=1.82−12=0.82
SD⁢[X] = 0.82=0.9055⁢….

3.1.3 Continuous Random Variables

  • •

    The probability density function (p.d.f) f of a continuous random variable X describes the probability density of each value, and is defined in the usual way:

    P⁢(X=x) = 0
    P⁢(x≤X≤x+d⁢x) ≈f⁢(x)⁢d⁢xfor small⁢d⁢x
    P⁢(a≤X≤b) =∫abf⁢(x)⁢𝑑x

Example: Continuous Random Variables

f⁢(x)={2⁢x0≤x≤10elsewhere

probability = area under f⁢(x)

P⁢(0.4≤X≤0.8)=∫0.40.82⁢x⁢𝑑x=0.82−0.42=0.48 (15)
  • •

    Often, a continuous random variable has a distribution that depends on external parameters.

Definition: The Normal Distribution

The Normal distribution, in its most general form, depends on two parameters: the mean μ and the standard deviation σ (or variance σ2). We say X∼N⁢(μ,σ2) and we denote its p.d.f. as

f⁢(x|μ,σ)=12⁢π⁢σ2⁢e−12⁢(x−μσ)2,−∞<x<∞. (16)
  • •

    Again, note the new notation in the distribution specified above: f⁢(x|μ,σ) to be read as “f of x given μ and σ”. For us to use the p.d.f. we really need to be told (i.e. given) μ and σ.

3.1.4 Expectation and Variance of Continuous Random Variables

  • •

    The expectation, variance, and standard deviation of a continuous random variable X with probability density function f⁢(x) are:

    E⁢[X] =∫x⁢f⁢(x)⁢𝑑x
    Var⁢[X] =E⁢[(X−E⁢[X])2]
    =E⁢[X2]−(E⁢[X])2 (with E⁢[X2]=∫x2⁢f⁢(x)⁢𝑑x)
    SD⁢[X] =Var⁢[X]

    where integration is over the full range of values of X.

Definition: The Uniform Distribution

A random variable X follows a uniform distribution on the interval [a,b] if the pdf is given by:

f⁢(x)={1b−afor⁢x∈[a,b],0otherwise. (17)

Example: The Uniform Distribution

  • •

    As a simple example, consider the uniform distribution on [0,1]. The pdf for X is f⁢(x)=1,   0≤x≤1, and f⁢(x)=0 outside this range of values.

  • •

    Notice that ∫011⁢𝑑x=1, as is required.

  • •

    We can find the probability that the random variable lies between 0.2 and 0.6 as ∫0.20.61⁢𝑑x=[x]0.20.6=0.4

  • •

    The random variable has expectation

    E⁢[X]=∫01x×1⁢𝑑x=[x22]01=12

    and variance

    Var⁢[X] = E⁢[X2]−(E⁢[X])2
    = ∫01x2×1⁢𝑑x−(E⁢[X])2
    = [x33]01−14=112

Definition: The Exponential Distribution

A random variable Y has an exponential distribution with parameter λ if

f⁢(y|λ)=λ⁢e−λ⁢y,   0≤y<∞.

Example: The Exponential Distribution

Let Y follow an exponential distribution with parameter λ=1, that is,

f⁢(y)=e−y,   0≤y<∞.
  • •

    Note total area is 1 (as it should be) because ∫0∞e−y⁢𝑑y=1.

  • •

    We can find the probability that the random variable lies between 0.2 and 0.6 as ∫0.20.6(e−y)⁢𝑑y=[−e−y]0.20.6=e−0.2−e−0.6=0.27

  • •

    The random variable has expectation

    E⁢[Y]=∫0∞(y)⁢(e−y)⁢𝑑y=1

    (after integrating by parts)

    and variance

    Var⁢[Y] = E⁢[Y2]−(E⁢[Y])2
    = ∫0∞(y2)⁢(e−y)⁢𝑑y−(E⁢[Y])2=2−12=1,

    after a little work.

3.1.5 Properties of Expectations and Variances

Change in Scale and Location

  • •

    Consider

    • –

      any random variable X,

    • –

      any two real numbers a and b.

  • •

    Then we have

    E⁢[a⁢X+b] =a⁢E⁢[X]+b
    Var⁢[a⁢X+b] =a2⁢Var⁢[X]
    SD⁢[a⁢X+b] =a⁢SD⁢[X]

Note

  • •

    Note that only the expectation changes due to b. As b only moves where the distribution is located, its shape/spread/variance/standard deviation is unaffected.

Covariance

  • •

    The covariance between two random variables X and Y is defined as:

    Cov⁢[X,Y] =E⁢[(X−E⁢[X])⁢(Y−E⁢[Y])]
    =E⁢[X⁢Y]−E⁢[X]⁢E⁢[Y]
  • •

    If two random variables X and Y are independent, then Cov⁢[X,Y]=0. However Cov⁢[X,Y]=0 does not imply independence.

Sums and Differences

  • •

    Consider any two random variables X and Y, and any two real numbers a and b.

  • •

    Then we have

    E⁢[a⁢X+b⁢Y]=a⁢E⁢[X]+b⁢E⁢[Y]
  • •

    If, additionally, X and Y are independent, then

    Var⁢[a⁢X+b⁢Y]=a2⁢Var⁢[X]+b2⁢Var⁢[Y]
  • •

    However, if X and Y are not independent, then

    Var⁢[a⁢X+b⁢Y]=a2⁢Var⁢[X]+b2⁢Var⁢[Y]+2⁢a⁢b⁢Cov⁢[X,Y]
  • •

    These rules can be extended to sums of several random variables.

  • •

    Consider any n random variables X1, X2, …, Xn

  • •

    Then

    E⁢[X1+X2+…+Xn]=E⁢[X1]+E⁢[X2]+…+E⁢[Xn]
  • •

    If, additionally, all Xi are independent of one another, then

    Var⁢[X1+X2+…+Xn]=Var⁢[X1]+Var⁢[X2]+…+Var⁢[Xn]

Example: Ice Cream 1

  • •

    An ice cream van sells ice creams made from a cornet and one scoop of each of vanilla and strawberry ice cream. Different scoops are used for different flavours. Each scoop is designed to scoop up 60 grams of ice cream, but there is some variation in the amount of ice cream scooped up: the typical error is 10 grams. The wafer cornets should weigh 10g, but have a typical error of 0.5g.
    What is the mean weight and standard deviation of an ice cream?

  • •

    notation

    • –

      I = weight of ice cream

    • –

      S1 = weight of scoop 1

    • –

      S2 = weight of scoop 2

    • –

      C = weight of cornet

  • •

    so I=S1+S2+C, hence

    E⁢[I]=E⁢[S1+S2+C]=E⁢[S1]+E⁢[S2]+E⁢[C]=60+60+10=130⁢g
  • •

    and additionally, assuming independence of S1, S2, and C (seems reasonable)

    SD⁢[I] =SD⁢[S1+S2+C]=Var⁢[S1+S2+C]
    =Var⁢[S1]+Var⁢[S2]+Var⁢[C]=SD⁢[S1]2+SD⁢[S2]2+SD⁢[C]2
    =2⁢(10)2+0.52=14.151⁢g
  • •

    note: one could take the view that the two scoops are not independent; in an extreme case, S1=S2; in this case:

    SD⁢[I] =SD⁢[2⁢S1+C]=Var⁢[2⁢S1+C]
    =4⁢Var⁢[S1]+Var⁢[C]=4⁢SD⁢[S1]2+SD⁢[C]2
    =4⁢(10)2+(0.5)2=20.006⁢g

    the “true” standard deviation will probably be somewhere in between these two values.

Example: Ice Cream 2

  • •

    Ice cream is held in the van in two tubs, each containing nominally 5Kg of ice cream before the first sale of the day. The actual quantity of ice cream in a tub is likely to be out by a small amount, typically plus or minus 15g.
    What is the mean weight and variance of the total amount of ice cream remaining in the two tubs following the first sale of the day?

  • •

    notation

    • –

      T1 = original weight in tub 1

    • –

      T2 = original weight in tub 2

    • –

      T1′ = weight in tub 1 after first sale

    • –

      T2′ = weight in tub 2 after first sale

  • •

    so T1′+T2′=T1−S1+T2−S2, hence

    E⁢[T1′+T2′]=E⁢[T1]−E⁢[S1]+E⁢[T2]−E⁢[S2]=10000⁢g−120⁢g=9880⁢g
  • •

    and additionally assuming independence of all variables involved (seems reasonable)

    SD⁢[T1′+T2′] =SD⁢[T1−S1+T2−S2]=Var⁢[T1−S1+T2−S2]
    =Var⁢[T1]+Var⁢[S1]+Var⁢[T2]+Var⁢[S2]
    =SD⁢[T1]2+SD⁢[S1]2+SD⁢[T2]2+SD⁢[S2]2
    =2⁢(15⁢g)2+2⁢(10⁢g)2=25.495⁢g
  • •

    note: again one could take the view that the two scoops are not independent; in an extreme case, S1=S2, and:

    SD⁢[T1′+T2′] =SD⁢[T1+T2−2⁢S1]=Var⁢[T1+T2−2⁢S1]
    =Var⁢[T1]+Var⁢[T2]+4⁢Var⁢[S1]
    =SD⁢[T1]2+SD⁢[T2]2+4⁢SD⁢[S1]2
    =2⁢(15⁢g)2+4⁢(10⁢g)2=29.155⁢g

    the “true” standard deviation will probably be somewhere in between these two values.

3.2 Random Sampling, Proportions and the Bernoulli Distribution

Motivating example 2: US Presidential Election Polling Pennsylvania State.

  • •

    It is the 22nd Oct 2024, two weeks before the 2024 US presidential election.

  • •

    You run a major polling company and you have conducted a large poll of people likely to vote across Pennsylvania State: a critical swing state in the election.

  • •

    Out of 1000 randomly chosen people 485 said they would vote for Harris, 515 for Trump (we will ignore “don’t knows/Libertarian party/Green Party” for now).

  • •

    Everyone wants to know your prediction: Multiple News networks keep calling (CNN, FOX etc), powerful Hedge funds are calling wanting an edge, calls from large military corporations are coming in too…

  • •

    What do you say about the possible result of the election? Do you trust what you would say? Would you bet on it?

  • •

    If you choose a person from Pennsylvania at random then they will have probability p of saying (truthfully) that they will vote for Trump, where p is the proportion of Trump voters in the state, so p=NT⁢r⁢u⁢m⁢p/N, with N the total voters in the state, but this value of p is totally unknown to us.

  • •

    We now set up a model for this situation which is very general and applies to a wide range of scientific experiments in addition to US Presidential elections.

3.2.1 The Bernoulli Distribution

  • •

    Perhaps the simplest type of experiment is one where there are only two possible outcomes such as

    • –

      Head or Tail (of a possibly unfair coin),

    • –

      success or failure,

    • –

      device is defective or nondefective,

    • –

      patient recovers or dies,

    • –

      Covid Vaccine effective for patient or not,

    • –

      person will vote for Trump, or will not.

  • •

    We designate the two possible outcomes of such an experiment as 0 and 1.

  • •

    The following definition can then be applied to every experiment of this form.

Definition: The Bernoulli Distribution

We say that a random variable X has a Bernoulli distribution with parameter p, satisfying 0≤p≤1, if X can take only the values 0 and 1 with respective probabilities

P⁢(X=1)=pandP⁢(X=0)= 1−p. (18)

Setting q=1−p we can write the p.m.f. as:

f⁢(x|p)={px⁢q1−xfor⁢x=0,1,0otherwise. (19)
  • •

    To see that f⁢(x|p) does indeed represent the Bernoulli distribution as given by the probabilities in (18); we can just note that

    f⁢(1|p)=pandf⁢(0|p)=q. (20)
  • •

    If X has a Bernoulli distribution with parameter p, then we can directly calculate its expectation and variance:

    E⁢[X] = ∑x=01x⁢f⁢(x|p)= 0.q+1.p=p (21)
    E⁢[X2] = ∑x=01x2⁢f⁢(x|p)= 02.q+12.p=p (22)
    Var⁢[X] = E⁢[X2]−E⁢[X]2 (23)
    = p−p2=p⁢(1−p)=p⁢q. (24)
  • •

    We can also calculate the moment generating function (m.g.f. - see probability course) as

    ψ⁢(t)=E⁢[et⁢X]=∑x=01et⁢x⁢f⁢(x|p)=q+p⁢etfor−∞<t<∞ (25)

3.2.2 Bernoulli Trials

  • •

    Related to our motivating examples, if we have a sequence of n random variables X1,…,Xn which are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.), and if each of the Xi has a Bernoulli distribution with parameter p, then we say that the variables X1,…,Xn form n Bernoulli trials with parameter p.

  • •

    We see that the concept of Bernoulli trials is a very useful model for describing many situations, for example:

    • –

      for the (unfair) coin that is flipped n times and gives a head with probability p, we simply set Xi=1 if a head is obtained on the ith flip and Xi=0 for a tail, with i=1,2,…,n.

    • –

      n people, each of whom have COVID (Xi=1) or do not (Xi=0).

    • –

      n machines, each of which is either defective (Xi=1) or is not (Xi=0).

Motivating example 2: US Presidential Election Polling Pennsylvania State: Sampling Without Replacement Approximation

  • •

    If you choose a person from Pennsylvania at random then they will have probability p of saying (truthfully) that they will vote for Trump, where p=NT⁢r⁢u⁢m⁢p/N is the proportion of Trump voters in the state, with N the total voters in the state. Whilst this value of p is totally unknown to us, it represents a true proportion.

Question: Can the concept of Bernoulli trials be used in the context of n voters, each of which either votes for Trump (Xi=1) or does not (Xi=0)?

  • •

    Well, without knowledge of any other vote, each of the sample of n voters will have probability p of voting for trump, i.e.

    P⁢(X1=1)=P⁢(X2=1)=…=P⁢(Xn=1)=p
  • •

    But are they independent?

  • •

    Well - almost! If I know Voter 1 voted for Trump (i.e. x1=1), then technically we have that the probability that Voter 2 voted for Trump given as

    P⁢(X2=1|X1=1)=NT⁢r⁢u⁢m⁢p−1N−1

    since Voter 1 has now been taken out of both the numerator (number of Trump voters) and denominator (total number of voters).

  • •

    However, if N (and NT⁢r⁢u⁢m⁢p) are large, this is still approximately NT⁢r⁢u⁢m⁢p/N.

  • •

    In particular, if N>>n, then this approximation will be sufficient for each of the sample of n voters, and hence we can (approximately) use the independent Bernoulli trials model for n voters, each of which either votes for Trump (Xi=1) or does not (Xi=0).

  • •

    Note that here we have shown that the sampling without replacement dependence is negligible, and approximate the situation as if we were sampling with replacement, hence, for a true SRS scheme we can assume independence of voters. In real-world scenarios, however, there can be dependence due to clustered sampling, households, social correlation, non-response, etc. (see Section 3.4 for further discussion).

3.2.3 Probability vs. Statistics

  • •

    This all seems fine, but we must keep in mind what we are interested in learning, and this highlights a common difference between Probability and Statistics.

  • •

    For a simple Probability question we may be told the probability p and be asked to calculate various probabilities of configurations of X1,…,Xn, e.g. their total.

  • •

    However, in Statistics we want to go a step further: following the form of a real world experiment, we would be told the results X1=x1,…,Xn=xn and then have to infer something meaningful about the unknown probability p.

  • •

    This process is generally referred to as inference about the parameter p, and we will discuss it far more rigorously later.

  • •

    Note that this is a somewhat simplified division between Probability and Statistics. Whilst this is instructive to think about, both subjects go much deeper into these issues!

3.2.4 Statistical Inference

  • •

    We should start by thinking about what p actually is (and this may depend on which example we are thinking about). We could view p as

    • (a)

      a single, real, fixed and “true” value that is unknown (this is more of a Frequentist view) - in this case we can’t make probability statements about the parameter itself, only the data.

    • (b)

      an unknown quantity about which we should represent our subjective uncertainty via a probability distribution (this is more of a Bayesian point of view: we will return to this later in the course).

  • •

    For viewpoint (a) (and somewhat also for (b)), we may seek to construct from the data X1,…,Xn some way of giving an estimate of p, and then subsequently examining the attributes of this estimator. We will set this up more formally for the general case later, but for now let us try it for the case of Bernoulli trials.

3.2.5 Totals and sample proportions as estimators

  • •

    First let us redefine the random quantity X to be the sum of all successes over n trials,

    X=∑i=1nXiwith⁢Xi={1when⁢i⁢is⁢a⁢success0when⁢i⁢is⁢a⁢failure (26)
  • •

    To guide us in estimating p, it is first worth noting what the p.m.f. is for a set of Bernoulli trials X1,…,Xn: as the Xi are independent we can then just multiply the individual p.m.f.s. Therefore

    f⁢(x1,x2,…,xn|p) = ∏i=1nf⁢(xi|p) (27)
    = ∏i=1npxi⁢q1−xi (28)
    = p∑i=1nxi⁢q∑i=1n(1−xi) (29)
    = px⁢qn−x (30)

    where we have now denoted x=∑i=1nxi to be the sum of the successes.

  • •

    It is interesting to see, rather intuitively, that this p.m.f. only depends on the probability p, the total number of Bernoulli trials n and the number of successes x. Hence perhaps we should construct an estimator for p using only n and x?

  • •

    We are in fact free to construct many types of estimator from combinations of the Xi, but some will be better than others. We can go further here, and ask what proposed or estimated value of p (which will be written in terms of Xi and n) will maximise the p.m.f. f⁢(x1,x2,…,xn|p) as given by equation (30): as surely this would give us a decent estimate of p? This will be in some sense the most “likely” value of p. Note that f⁢(x1,x2,…,xn|p) viewed as a function of p with data fixed (e.g. already collected) is often referred to as the likelihood: more on this topic and its slightly subtle definition later.

  • •

    We use the trick of maximising the log of f⁢(x1,x2,…,xn|p), as this is a little easier to differentiate:

    f⁢(x1,x2,…,xn|p) = px⁢qn−x (31)
    ⇒log⁡f⁢(x1,x2,…,xn|p) = x⁢log⁡p+(n−x)⁢log⁡(1−p) (32)
    ⇒∂∂p⁢log⁡f⁢(x1,x2,…,xn|p) = xp−n−x1−p (33)

    therefore an estimate for p, which we denote p^, which maximises f⁢(x1,x2,…,xn|p) is given by

    xp^−n−x1−p^ = 0 (34)
    ⇒x⁢(1−p^) = (n−x)⁢p^ (35)
    ⇒x−x⁢p^ = n⁢p^−x⁢p^ (36)
    ⇒x = n⁢p^ (37)
    ⇒p^ = xn (38)
  • •

    So this suggests that we should take the proportion of successes out of our n trials as our estimate for the true probability p. This is a very intuitive/obvious result! (Note that the above mathematical machinery, a process known as maximising the likelihood, is very general and very powerful: more on this later.)

  • •

    This estimate p^ is often also called the sample proportion Y, and in terms of random variables we would write:

    p^=Y=Xn=1n⁢∑i=1nXi (39)

    where Y is simply the proportion of successes in our set (or sample) of Bernoulli trials of size n. We will use the notation p^ and Y interchangeably: they each have strengths.

  • •

    Note that p^=Y can also be considered as simply the mean of the Xi: a point we shall return to.

  • •

    In fact, we anticipate that Y should “tend to” the probability p as n gets larger, as a result of the Weak Law of Large Numbers (see Probability course). Consequently, it should provide a good “guess” for p, but we want to know how good a guess it actually is for finite values of n (like those we experience in the real world!).

  • •

    In this case we can go a lot further, and ask what is the precise probability mass function of X (and hence trivially for Y too)?

3.2.6 The Binomial Distribution

  • •

    A very important distribution, which you will already be familiar with, is as follows.

Definition: The Binomial Distribution

A random variable X has a binomial distribution with parameters n and p if X has a discrete distribution for which the p.m.f. is as follows:

f⁢(x|n,p)={(nx)⁢px⁢qn−xfor⁢x=0,1,2,…,n,0otherwise. (40)

Here n must be a positive integer and p must lie in the interval 0≤p≤1. We write X∼B⁢i⁢n⁢(n,p). The Binomial distribution is of fundamental importance to us because of the following result:

If the collection of random variables X1,…,Xn form n Bernoulli trials with parameter p, and if X=X1+⋯+Xn represents the sum of the successes, then X has a binomial distribution with parameters n and p.

  • •

    The Binomial distribution was proved in the Probability course in Michaelmas term, but essentially it just gathers together all the (nx) orderings of the Bernoulli trials X1,…,Xn that have the same total number of successes X.

Discussion: form of the Binomial distribution

Compare the Binomial distribution’s form to that of the Bernoulli distribution as given by equation (19). Note their inevitable agreement when n=1, as the sum of a single Bernoulli trial is of course equivalent to a single Bernoulli trial. Compare also the Binomial distribution’s form with the p.m.f. of the n Bernoulli trials f⁢(x1,x2,…,xn|p) as given by Equation (30). Note the missing (nx) factor in the latter. This is because for f⁢(x1,x2,…,xn|p) the particular ordering of the successes is specified, and hence there is only one way to do this. However for the Binomial case we just have f⁢(x|n,p), where x=x1+x2+⋯+xn is just the total number of successes, and hence the order of successes has been ‘forgotten’. Therefore we must group together the (nx) possible ways of ordering x successes in n trials.

  • •

    When X is viewed as the sum of n Bernoulli trials in this way, the values of its expectation, variance and m.g.f. can be easily found using those of the Bernoulli distribution, given by equations (21) and (24):

    E⁢[X] = ∑i=1nE⁢[Xi]=n⁢p, (41)
    Var⁢[X] = ∑i=1nVar⁢[Xi]=n⁢p⁢q, (42)
    ψ⁢(t) = E⁢[et⁢X]=∏i=1nE⁢[et⁢Xi]=(p⁢et+q)n (43)

    (in the last line we used property M4 from the Probability course: that the m.g.f. of a sum of independent random variables is just the product of the individual m.g.f.s).

  • •

    Note a subtlety here: the above expectation and variance of X are as usual calculated from a view point before X is actually measured.

  • •

    As we now understand the behaviour of the total number of successes X (in that we have its distribution, expectation, variance, m.g.f. etc.), we similarly understand our estimator p^=Y=X/n of the probability (or proportion) p.

Aside: Normal approximation to Binomial and Continuity Correction

  • •

    We know X∼B⁢i⁢n⁢(n,p), but sometimes this can be cumbersome to calculate probabilities with.

  • •

    As you saw in the Probability course, we can approximate the binomial distribution by a Normal distribution with the same mean and variance:

    B⁢i⁢n⁢(n,p)⁢ is approximately ⁢N⁢(n⁢p,n⁢p⁢(1−p))
  • •

    This approximation is acceptable when n⁢p≥10⁢ and ⁢n⁢(1−p)≥10, and the larger these values the better.

  • •

    For smallish n, a continuity correction might be appropriate; that is, if X∼Bin⁢(n,p) and X′∼N⁢(n⁢p,n⁢p⁢(1−p)), then

    P⁢(X≤k) ≃P⁢(X′≤k+1/2)
    P⁢(k1≤X≤k2) ≃P⁢(k1−1/2≤X′≤k2+1/2)

3.3 The Sample Proportion as an Estimator for p

  • •

    We can now finally say something about how ‘good’ our sample proportion estimator p^=Y=X/n is for estimating the true proportion p (knowledge of which would tell us if Trump wins Pennsylvania). As X∼B⁢i⁢n⁢(n,p) we have that:

    E⁢[p^]=E⁢[Y] = E⁢[Xn]=1n⁢E⁢[X] (44)
    = 1n⁢n⁢p=p (45)
    Var⁢[p^]=Var⁢[Y] = Var⁢[Xn]=1n2⁢Var⁢[X] (46)
    = 1n2⁢n⁢p⁢q=p⁢qn=p⁢(1−p)n (47)
  • •

    We have E⁢[p^]=p, that is the expectation of our estimator p^ is equal to the thing it is trying to estimate! We say that such an estimator is unbiased: arguably a desirable property, although mainly just from a Frequentist point of view.

  • •

    As we have Var⁢[p^]=p⁢(1−p)/n we now have some understanding and some control over how accurate our estimate is: if we double the size of the sample n then the variance will halve. Note that the corresponding standard deviation SD⁢[p^]=p⁢(1−p)/n would only change by a factor of 1/2 though.

Normal Approximation

  • •

    As X∼B⁢i⁢n⁢(n,p) and Y=X/n, we can calculate probabilities for Y=p^ (if we are given n and p say), but if n is large this is cumbersome.

  • •

    We can instead employ the Normal approximation for X (as discussed above) and then:

    X ∼ B⁢i⁢n⁢(n,p) (48)
    ⇒X ∼ N⁢(n⁢p,n⁢p⁢(1−p))(approximately, for n⁢p and n⁢(1−p) large)
    ⇒p^=Y ∼ N⁢(p,p⁢(1−p)n) (49)
  • •

    We can also use the continuity correction discussed at the end of Section 3.2.6 to improve this approximation if necessary.

Margin of Error

  • •

    So how accurate is our estimator Y? The Margin of Error of an estimate can be roughly defined (for now) as two22 2 Why two? As we shall discuss more later, 95% of the probability mass of a normal distribution is contained within 1.96 (i.e. ≈2) standard deviations of the mean. standard deviations, i.e. 2⁢SD⁢[Y], on either side of the estimate, suggesting the true value p may lie in an interval of the form:

    Y± 2⁢p⁢(1−p)n (50)

    This is unfortunately pretty useless, because usually we don’t know p: if we did, there would be no point in estimating it in the first place! (Note also that this interval is very informal: we will improve on this in the next section when we discuss Confidence Intervals.)

  • •

    However, we can find a very useful upper bound on the margin of error, because we have that:

    maxp∈[0,1]⁡p⁢(1−p)=14atp=12 (51)

    (you can find this by differentiating, or noting that p⁢(1−p) is a quadratic with roots at 0 and 1). Therefore,

    Margin of Error=2⁢p⁢(1−p)n≤  2⁢14⁢n=1n (52)

    We therefore have that the margin of error is bounded by 1/n no matter what the value of p. From Equation (50), a conservative error-bound interval can then be given by:

    Y±1n (53)

    We will go on to formalise these ideas in the next section of the course.

  • •

    The upper bound on the margin of error given by Inequality (52) is incredibly useful (as it doesn’t depend on p). However, once data has been observed, we could also approximate the standard deviation SD⁢[Y], and hence margin of error, by substituting in the observed estimate p^ for the population proportion. We would then have an estimate for SD⁢[Y], given by

    SD⁢[Y]^=p^⁢(1−p^)n (54)

    and hence could estimate the Margin of Error to be 2⁢p^⁢(1−p^)n. This approximation gets better as n gets larger.

  • •

    We can now answer many questions about the US Presidential Election (but not all!).

Example: Predicting US Presidential Election Polling

  • •

    It is 22nd Oct 2024 and your company’s poll of 1000 randomly chosen people from Pennsylvania, from Motivating Example 2, is about to be performed tomorrow.

  • •

    Let X equal the number of people who may say they will vote for Trump (so Xi=1 for an individual Trump voter).

  • •

    Question 1: find the expected value and margin of error for the proportion of Trump voters in our sample if we were (magically) told that the true value is (a) p=0.5 or (b) p=0.3.

  • •

    Answer 1(a): If p=0.5 then the expected value of X is E⁢[X]=n⁢p=1000×0.5=500 and the expected sample proportion p^ is E⁢[p^]=p=0.5=50%. The variances are Var⁢[X]=n⁢p⁢(1−p)=1000×0.5×0.5=250 so SD⁢[X]=15.8 people, and Var⁢[p^]=p⁢(1−p)/n=0.5×0.5/1000=0.00025 and margin of error =2⁢p⁢(1−p)/n=2⁢0.5×0.5/1000=0.0316 (to 3 s.f.)=3.16%

  • •

    Answer 1(b): Similar calculations for the p=0.3 case yield: E⁢[X]=300, E⁢[p^]=p=0.3=30%. Var⁢[X]=210 so SD⁢[X]=14.5 people, and Var⁢[p^]=0.00021 and margin of error =2⁢p⁢(1−p)/n=0.0290 (to 3 s.f.)=2.90%

  • •

    Note that the margin of error narrows as p moves away from 0.5.

  • •

    Question 2: It is the 22nd Oct 2024 and the poll of size n=1000 is performed with results: 485 said they would vote for Harris and 515 for Trump. We are not (magically) told what p is: it is unknown. What is your estimate for p? What is a) the corresponding (upper bound on the) margin of error, and b) the estimated (from the data) margin of error?

  • •

    Answer 2: We use the sample proportion as our estimate for p which is

    p^=xn=5151000= 0.515= 51.5%(to 3 s.f.) (55)

    a) We do not know p so we could use the maximum bound for the margin of error:

    1n=11000=0.0316227⁢…=0.0316=3.16%(to 3 s.f.) (56)

    so we may anticipate (in some sense) that the true proportion p is likely to lie in the interval:

    51.5%±3.16% (57)

    Note that the all important value of p=0.5=50%, the boundary between a Trump victory/loss, is still within this interval (i.e. within the margin of error).

    b) If we approximate SD⁢[Y] by utilising our observed estimate p^ in place of p, we obtain an approximation for the margin of error given by

    2⁢p^⁢(1−p^)n=2⁢0.515×0.4851000=0.0316085⁢…=0.0316=3.16%(to 3 s.f.) (58)

    Note that this is very similar to (and the same to 3 s.f.) the upper bound calculated above (in part 2a)). These answers are close in this case since the estimate p^=0.515 is close to the value p=0.5 which maximises p⁢(1−p) as stated by Equation (51).

  • •

    Question 3: Your company has time to perform one more poll before the election. You see that Pennsylvania is currently “too close to call”. How large a poll would your company have to perform to ensure a margin of error less than 1%?

  • •

    Answer 3: To ensure the (upper bound of the) margin of error is less than 1% or 0.01 we must have:

    1n< 0.01⇔n>10.012⇔n> 10000 (59)

    So a poll larger than n=10000 is required: expensive stuff, but it may indeed be worth it!

The actual Pennsylvania votes were: 3,542,701 Donald Trump (Republican), 3,421,247 Kamala Harris (Democrat), 34,513 Jill Stein (Green), 33,309 Chase Oliver (Libertarian), which implies 0.5087202 for Trump and 0.4912798 for Harris (removing 3rd and 4th parties).

3.4 Why are Opinion Polls So Often Wrong?

  • •

    Many opinion polls take samples of about 1000, and as shown above, this gives a margin of error of about 11000=0.0316, or about 3%, a widely quoted figure.

  • •

    So why do so many opinion polls give, or seem to give, “wrong” estimates? This would require several books to discuss, but there are a few obvious reasons.

    1. 1.

      Doubts about whether the sample was statistically representative of the population.

    2. 2.

      Doubts about the truthfulness of the response.

    3. 3.

      There is a difference between how the general public interpret opinion polls, and how statisticians interpret them. In particular, opinion poll estimates and margins of error reported are not probabilities. We will see why this is so shortly.

Summary of Frequentist Methods in Section 3

It is worth summarising the core structure that we have developed in this section, as it possesses many of the pieces of a general Frequentist analysis.

  • •

    Working in the Frequentist framework, there was an unknown but fixed property of the world p that we wished to learn about.

  • •

    This represented the proportion of Trump voters in the US Presidential Polling example, which is equivalent to the probability of a randomly selected individual being a Trump voter, but it could equally have represented the probability of rolling a 6 on a loaded dice, or of flipping a Head on an unfair coin: our structure applies to all of these cases.

  • •

    We get the results from a random (this is critically important!) sample X1,…,Xn of size n with Xi=0,1 of size n, which contains some necessarily incomplete information about the parameter p.

  • •

    We linked the behaviour of the sample to the possible values of p via probabilistic statements such as Xi∼B⁢e⁢r⁢n⁢o⁢u⁢l⁢l⁢i⁢(p) and X∼B⁢i⁢n⁢(n,p).

  • •

    Using a maximum likelihood argument, we constructed, from the sample, an estimator p^=Y=X/n that should be good at estimating the key parameter of interest p.

  • •

    We examined its properties to ensure that it was good: unbiased E⁢[p^]=p, with controllable variance Var⁢[p^]=p⁢(1−p)/n and known distribution (via X).

  • •

    We noted that the estimator p^=Y=X/n is actually equal to the sample mean.

  • •

    We found for larger n that the distribution of the estimator p^=Y could be approximated by a Normal distribution: p^=Y∼N⁢(p,p⁢(1−p)/n).

  • •

    Given actual data, we could then estimate p and provide intervals based on an approximate Margin of Error argument (this needs making more formal!).

  • •

    We could even assume a particular value of p, and then calculate how extreme certain data was given this assumption (see Question 9 on the Problem Sheet).

  • •

    Big Question: Does the above Frequentist structure generalise to more complex situations, e.g. where Xi doesn’t just equal 0 or 1, and/or where the Xi are generated by alternative, more complex probability distributions?

  • •

    Answer: A million times yes.
